**Key points:**

You comparison shopped and chose your mortgage lender carefully. Then, shortly after closing, you received a letter from a new company introducing itself as your servicing provider. What does this change mean?


Having your loan sold to a new servicer may raise questions, particularly with[first-time homebuyers](https://www.pennymac.com/purchasing/first-time-homebuyer-guide) . You may be wondering: Is your lender allowed to do this? Will your carefully budgeted payment amount suddenly change? Here’s what you need to know about your mortgage being sold to another company.


## What It Means When Your Mortgage Is Sold


To understand what it means when your mortgage is sold, let’s start by reviewing the entities involved with the funding and maintenance of your home loan.


When you obtain a mortgage, you may end up working with two types of entities: mortgage originators and mortgage servicers.


- **Mortgage originators.** These are the companies or institutions (like banks or mortgage lenders) that help you secure your loan. They handle tasks like processing your application, underwriting and funding the loan.
- **Mortgage servicers.** After your loan closes, it enters the servicing phase. Servicers manage the administrative side of your mortgage, including payment collection and escrow management.


Borrowers may work with a certain originator initially, and a separate or different servicer thereafter, unless the originator also provides servicing, as Pennymac does.


When you’ve been notified that your mortgage has been sold, it often means that the servicing rights for your loan have been transferred to a new company. This means you’ll send your monthly payments to a new servicer, who will handle the day-to-day management of your loan, such as collecting payments, managing escrow accounts and providing customer service.


## Why Do Mortgage Companies Sell Your Loan?


There are a few primary reasons why mortgages get sold.


### A Mortgage Originator May Not Service Loans


Many mortgage originators do not service loans and, as a result, sell your loan shortly after it funds to a mortgage servicer.


However, some companies, such as Pennymac, originate and service mortgages. In this case, your loan remains with your originator after it funds, and you retain the relationship with your lender (often for the life of your loan).


### To Free Up Capital


Lenders often sell or[transfer mortgages](https://www.pennymac.com/blog/explaining-the-loan-process-epilogue-transfer-of-loan-servicing) to free up capital, converting long-term loans into immediate cash. This practice allows them to meet federal cash reserve requirements and continue offering new loans to other borrowers.


### Reduce Risks


Many mortgage lenders sell loans because they are not administratively equipped to deal with the entirely different set of laws, regulations and procedures that apply to the servicing of a mortgage, and want to avoid the risk, responsibility and cost of taking on that task. For example, servicers must handle escrow accounts, lender-placed insurance, loss mitigation procedures, disclosures and payment processing, as well as defaults and delinquent accounts.


## Why Do Mortgages Get Sold More Than Once?


A mortgage may be sold more than once for several reasons, including:


- **Resale in the secondary market.** Loans are often bundled and sold to investors, who may later sell them again based on their financial strategy.
- **Evolving market conditions.** Shifts in interest rates or investor demand can lead to loans being bought and sold to better align with portfolio goals.
- **Company mergers or restructuring.** When lenders or investors change their business structure, loans can be transferred as part of a larger transaction.
- **Changes in participating parties.** As the loan moves through its lifecycle, it may pass between investors or institutions with different priorities.


These changes typically happen behind the scenes, and even if your mortgage is transferred multiple times, your loan terms remain the same. It’s still important to review any transfer notices and keep records for your reference.


## What Changes When Your Mortgage Is Sold?


If you’re notified that your mortgage has been sold, the good news is that in most cases very little actually changes for you.


Here’s what may change:


- **Where you send your monthly payment.** Payments will go to your new loan servicer.
- **Your customer service contact.** You’ll reach out to a new company for questions or support.
- **Your online account platform.** You will likely need to set up a new online account with your new servicer.


What *doesn’t* change:


- **Your loan terms stay the same.** Your interest rate, loan balance and repayment schedule remain unchanged.
- **Your monthly payment doesn’t change because of the transfer.** Any changes to your payment would happen regardless of a transfer.


- For example, payments may adjust if you have an[adjustable-rate mortgage](https://www.pennymac.com/adjustable-rate-mortgages-arms) (ARM).
- Payments can also change due to factors like property taxes or mortgage insurance, which has nothing to do with your loan being sold.


## Who Owns Your Mortgage?


There is an important distinction here: neither the company that originated your loan nor the servicer may actually own your loan.


Today, a large percentage of home loans are purchased from lenders by government-sponsored entities like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. This helps free up capital in the mortgage lending space, enabling lenders to provide financing for more individuals seeking mortgages.


In other instances, a home loan may be held by a portfolio lender or purchased by private investors in the secondary market. These privately purchased loans are often bundled into mortgage-backed securities (MBS).


- MBS containing[FHA](https://www.pennymac.com/fha-home-loans) ,[VA](https://www.pennymac.com/va-home-loans) and USDA loans are generally guaranteed by Ginnie Mae
- MBS made up of conventional loans are typically guaranteed by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac


Regardless of the scenario, the purchaser becomes the official loan owner, even if another company is responsible for loan servicing.


## What to Do If Your Mortgage Was Sold to Another Lender


Remember, when your mortgage is sold, the terms of your loan remain unchanged. Staying informed and proactive can help ensure a smooth transition and avoid potential issues.


### Verify Your New Servicer Information


Make sure you have the correct details for your new servicer, including:


- Customer service number
- Mailing address
- Online account portal


### Update Automatic Payments


If you previously set up automatic payments, you’ll need to:


- Set up automatic payments with your new servicer and confirm when your first payment is due
- Cancel your old payment arrangements only after the new one is confirmed


This includes updating the account number, billing address and company name. Your new servicer should provide everything needed to complete this step.


### Set Up Your New Online Account


Switching servicers may mean setting up a new online account. Since not all servicers offer the same features, you may need to adjust how you manage your loan based on the tools your new servicer provides. Check what’s available in terms of:


- Online payments
- Paperless statements
- Account management tools


### Confirm Account Details


During the transition, confirm that everything has been correctly transferred to your new account:


- Payment information
- Escrow account details
- Loan balance and account information


### Keep Good Records


Hold onto mortgage statements from both before and after the transfer. These records can help:


- Confirm payments were made on time
- Resolve any disputes or discrepancies


### Watch for Timing Issues


Be mindful of timing if your loan is in transition during other processes:


- **Loan modification:** You should not have to restart the process, but keep detailed records of all documents and communications to avoid delays.
- **Refinancing:** Notify your new lender right away if your current loan is transferred so they can ensure the correct payoff amount is used. Keep in mind, until your refinance closes, you’re still responsible for making payments on your existing mortgage. Once it closes, your original loan is paid off and replaced with a new one. After closing, any transfer notices related to your original loan no longer apply, since it has been fully paid off.


## Borrower Rights When Your Mortgage Is Sold


As a mortgagor, you do have certain rights. Similarly, the lender, or mortgagee, has legal and fiduciary responsibilities to ensure you are treated fairly. Some of those rights include:


- **The right to be notified of a transfer.** Your current lender must provide a loan ownership transfer notice before your loan moves to a new servicer. If ownership of your loan changes, the new owner must notify you separately.
- **The right to clear information from your new servicer (at least 15 days before the effective transfer date), including:**


- How to contact your new servicer (name, address, phone number)
- How to contact your current servicer
- The last day your current servicer will accept payments and the first day the new servicer will
- Whether the transfer affects any optional insurance (like mortgage, life or disability insurance) and what you need to do to keep your coverage
- Confirmation that the transfer does not change your loan terms


- **The right to a 60-day grace period.** If you send a payment to your previous servicer by mistake during this time, it cannot be treated as late or reported to credit bureaus.


You also have the right to accurate information. Review all communication from your new servicer carefully, and contact them right away if anything looks incorrect.


## Mortgage Sales Frequently Asked Questions


### Why wasn’t I asked permission?


Your mortgage can be sold without your consent and may be sold multiple times. However, lenders are required to disclose when the sale has occurred.


### Can I prevent or refuse the sale of my mortgage?


As a homeowner, you cannot prevent your mortgage from being sold or transferred. Lenders have the legal right to sell loans to other entities, lenders or investors under federal law and the terms outlined in your loan contract. But remember that mortgage selling is standard in the industry, and your loan terms will remain the same as they were when you took out your mortgage.


### What if I have an issue with the new mortgage servicing company?


If you have an issue with your new mortgage servicing company, contact them and discuss your problem. Include your name, account number and contact details when describing your issue. If sending a letter, the servicer must acknowledge receipt within five business days and respond with a resolution or next steps within 30 business days. While you cannot choose your servicing company, you do have rights. Visit the[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau website](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1024/33/) for more information on current regulations regarding mortgage servicing transfers.


### Why would my mortgage loan be transferred?


Mortgages are often transferred or sold to free up funds for lenders to issue new loans, allowing them to continue lending to other borrowers while another entity services your loan.


Your mortgage may also be transferred or sold because your particular lender is solely a mortgage originator, meaning they set up loans but do not handle the ongoing servicing. Mortgage servicers specialize in managing tasks like collecting monthly payments, handling escrow accounts, and providing customer support for the loan duration.


### Is it bad for a lender to sell your mortgage?


While there are generally no negative implications if your mortgage is sold, it does mean keeping track of where to make payments and stay on top of whether a new servicer has taken over the loan. Unless you originate with a lender who also handles servicing (such as Pennymac), transfers are just part of how the industry functions. The sale process keeps the mortgage market active and ensures a continuous flow of funds for new homebuyers and homeowners.


## It Pays to Pay Attention to Your Mortgage


The freedom to sell loans allows lenders and servicers to remain stable and profitable — freeing up more funds for homebuyers like you. If your loan is sold, be proactive with questions and organized with your new payment information. Attention to this quick and easy process makes for a smoother transition for you and your new mortgage servicer.
